The Fifth Amendment Show

Anthony Fauci spent 54 years in government service, much of it testifying before Congress. 

On Wednesday, he sat back down and said nothing at all, pleading the Fifth dozens of times to Rand Paul and every other senator who asked, opening with, "Under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions," The Washington Post reported. 

Josh Hawley asked him what day it was and what color his tie was. 

Fauci pleaded the Fifth to that too. When your legal strategy is silence on the weather, you've stopped performing accountability theater and started performing something closer to installation art.

Paul, who has spent years building a career on Fauci-shaped grievance, ended the nearly three-hour hearing threatening a contempt vote, even while acknowledging to his own GOP colleagues that Biden's preemptive pardon of Fauci raises real legal questions about whether contempt would even hold up. 

His underlying position, as the Post described it, was that Fauci should have simply answered the questions on Wednesday regardless of what it might have exposed. 

Fauci's lawyer tried to respond to that on the record and got escorted out by Capitol Police for the trouble, offering only a "Buh-bye" on his way to the door.

Here's the part everyone in that room already understood and nobody said out loud: this hearing was never designed to produce an answer, it was designed to produce a clip. 

Paul gets a viral moment of Fauci going silent on camera. Hawley gets his "narcissist and megalomaniac" soundbite next to a decommissioned magazine cover. 

Fauci's 150-scientist open letter gets to call the whole spectacle "absurd charges" driven by "conspiracy theories" that have brought "a five-year period of harassment and threats of violence" against him and his family.

 Democrats on the committee get to canonize Fauci as a martyr scientist. 

Every single participant walked in already knowing exactly what footage they wanted to walk out with, and every single one of them got it, including Paul, who has spent five years publicly saying Fauci should end up, in Fauci's own paraphrase, "behind bars."

Meanwhile the actual public verdict was rendered months before anyone sat down at that table. 

A 2025 Economist/YouGov poll found 57 percent of Americans think it's probably or definitely true the virus leaked from a Chinese lab, per the same reporting, and the Trump White House has already built a government website declaring the lab leak the "true" origin, without offering the proof it promises. 

Congress spent three hours performing a search for truth about a question the country, and apparently the executive branch, already stopped debating. 

So who exactly was this hearing for: the senators asking questions, the one witness answering none of them, or the millions of people who'd already made up their minds before the gavel came down?

🔔 Ethereum price faces $2,000 test as oil surge revives rate fears 

⚡️ Ethereum price has remained trapped below $2,000 as rising oil prices, renewed interest-rate concerns and BitMEX’s planned shutdown have tempered bullish sentiment despite continued spot ETF inflows. According to data from cryptonews, Ethereum price traded near $1,927 on July 23 after reaching an intraday high of $1,941. The token has recovered more than 27% from its June low near $1,514, but repeated failures around $1,955 have kept the psychological $2,000 level beyond buyers’ reach.

🔗 Rate traders have already adjusted their positions. The probability of a September Fed hike rose to 79% from 68% per data from the CME FedWatch tool. Expectations for the July meeting remain centered on no change, but another oil-led inflation increase could lift Treasury yields and pressure risk assets such as Ethereum. 

🔖 U.S. equities also weakened after Alphabet raised its 2026 capital-spending forecast to between $195 billion and $205 billion. The company recorded negative free cash flow of $5.9 billion as quarterly expenditure doubled to $44.9 billion, while its shares fell in premarket trading.

🇺🇦📈 The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) has raised its key policy rate, revised its inflation forecast upwards, and commented on the impact of port blockades.

Today, July 30th, the NBU's board decided to raise its key policy rate by 0.5% to 15.5% per annum, announced NBU Chairman Andriy Pyshnyi, citing rising inflation.

"Given the sustained increase in underlying inflationary pressures and a more significant acceleration in overall inflation towards the end of the year".
He acknowledged that in recent months, the increase in "underlying inflationary pressures" has taken on the characteristics of a persistent trend due to rising business costs:

➡️ In logistics.
➡️In labor costs.
➡️ In energy resources.

The head of the NBU reported a deterioration in the inflation forecast – from 9.4% to 10% by the end of 2026, and from 6.5% to 6.9% by the end of 2027.

"In recent weeks, the risks associated with the war in the Middle East have also increased. Oil prices have begun to rise again after a period of decline. Further escalation of the war in the Middle East could exacerbate the negative consequences for the Ukrainian economy. In addition, this could worsen the international security situation and simultaneously increase Russia's ability to continue the full-scale war," said Andriy Pyshnyi.
He also predicted an increase in demand for foreign currency in Ukraine, linked to defense needs.

"The forecast takes into account the increased need for imports of components for the production of weapons, and accordingly, an expansion of structural demand for foreign currency, which will require the NBU to increase its interventions to meet the needs of the economy and, at the same time, maintain the stability of the foreign exchange market," Pyshnyi said.
In practice, this means that the NBU will sell even more dollars on the interbank market from its gold and foreign exchange reserves.

Pyshnyi also acknowledged the negative impact of military strikes on Ukrainian seaports on Ukrainian exports, particularly agricultural exports. According to his estimates, the total volume of agricultural exports was still $4-4.5 billion per month, and 90% of it went through seaports. According to NBU estimates, these supplies are now being partially redirected to rail and the Danube ports (although in smaller volumes due to shallow water), but this will not be able to fully solve the problem.

Pyshnyi estimated the volume of lost revenue for the agricultural sector (due to the port blockades) at $2.5 billion per month, and predicted a reduction in foreign exchange earnings for agricultural exporters to $2-2.5 billion per month.

"The exchange rate will not skyrocket. The NBU controls the exchange rate regime," Pyshnyi promised. 

The NBU identified the following key economic risks related to the war:

➡️The emergence of additional budget needs to support defense and reconstruction, and to expand domestic demand, including imports.
➡️ Increased pressure on wages due to a deepening shortage of labor and negative migration trends.

The key policy rate will not be reviewed in August 2026. The next meeting of the NBU's board on monetary policy issues is scheduled for September 17th.
